##### Application

[RibbonApplicationTabScope](./application-tab/index.md#ribbon-application-tab-scope)

#### Commands

A command button is one of two sizes, and each tab says which of its commands are which:

- full: its small icon above its label, centred, exactly two slim buttons stacked tall
- slim: 27 pixels tall, its small icon to the left of its label
- small: only in the collapsed ribbon: 22 pixels tall, its small icon to the left of its label, and only as wide as they are

Buttons side by side are 4 pixels apart. Slim buttons side by side stack down instead, top aligned, two to a column, 4 pixels apart, each column as wide as its widest button and each button as wide as its column; a third starts the next column, 4 pixels along. A button's label is in the regular text colour, its icon beside or above it in the same colour, with 8 pixels either side of them. A full button always stands alone. A slim button fills only its column's width: nowhere does a button stretch to fill a row.
Every command starts from the top of its group, so the commands of a tab all start at the same line. A full button is always two slim buttons stacked tall, never shorter or taller, however much its icon and label would take, alone or beside any column.
Every button is square, with no rounded corners, and no border. Its background is clearly apart from the commands' area behind it, though still quiet: #444444 on the #222222 area in dark mode, white laid about an eighth of the way over the area, and not quite half way in light mode, rather than a colour of its own, so it stays as far apart from a tinted body too, lighter in both modes, and more so while hovered; while pressed it darkens instead. An on or off setting, like dark mode, is a switch rather than a button, and has no background of its own: the switch and its label sit straight on the commands' area, with nothing behind them, as wide as a button of its size and as tall as the switch and its label need.
A command's tooltip explains what it does rather than repeating its label, and gives its keyboard shortcut if it has one.
A command can be marked primary; each tab says which of its commands are.
A command that can't run is disabled, not hidden, and its tooltip says why.

#### Height

The commands drive the height: the command area is as tall as the tallest column of the open tabs, padded 8 pixels above and below, and nothing more. Since no column holds more than two slim buttons, and a full button is two slim buttons tall, the tallest the command area gets is two slim buttons with 4 pixels between them, padded: 74 pixels, and never more. A tab whose tallest column is two slim buttons, or that has a full button, is taller than one of a single slim button, and a tab with no commands, which is only its "No commands yet" padded the same way, is the shortest of all. So switching tabs can change the command area's height, and the window beneath moves with it.
There are 8 pixels of padding at either end, and "No commands yet" keeps 8 pixels from the left edge too.

#### Collapsing

The ribbon collapses, and expands again, with a chevron button in the left container, after the project indicator, by double-clicking a tab, or with Ctrl+F1 (Cmd+F1 on macOS). Whether it is collapsed is one of the [UserPreferencesScope](../../../scope/user-preferences/index.md#user-preferences-scope).
The chevron button is square, 22 pixels on each side, its icon centred in it. It is the same size, and its icon the same size, whether the ribbon is expanded or collapsed: only the way the chevron points changes.
Collapsed, the tabs go away too. The ribbon becomes a single thin row, exactly as tall as the row of tabs is when expanded, its bottom line where the tab row's is, so collapsing or expanding moves nothing above that line, led by the left container, the same as beside the tabs, the project indicator filling the row's height, and then every primary command, from all of the tabs, as small buttons: a small icon beside its label, and dark mode as a small switch with no background, only as wide as it and its label. Every one is only as wide as its own icon and label, 8 pixels from the next, whatever the tab it comes from calls it; a command that is slim in its tab doesn't grow to fill the row. They keep the order of their tabs, with a thin vertical divider between the commands of one tab and the next, and keep their tooltips and disabled states. The right container, when it holds anything, ends the row. Every control in the row, the dividers and the containers' contents included, is vertically centred in it.
When the commands and dividers are wider than the room between the left container and the right container, or the right end of the row, that stretch of the row scrolls sideways, as the expanded command area does. The containers stay where they are, never scrolled away or squeezed, and nothing in the row shrinks to fit.

1200	## 11. Belay: the agentic framework
1201	
1202	Belay is bundled as `@piton/belay`. It gives Piton a vocabulary for agents and
1203	compiles it into the artifacts that agentic coding tools read. The division of
1204	labour:
1205	
1206	- **Piton** handles parsing, evaluation, imports, exports, inheritance,
1207	  reachability and the renderers.
1208	- **Belay** adds the constructs and the adapters that turn them into files for
1209	  each platform.
1210	- The **consuming platform** executes the result. Successful compilation is
1211	  not proof of correct agent execution.
1212	
1213	Besides the four constructs, Belay provides `belay-config`, the adapters and
1214	the special imports.
1215	
1216	Source authority: lasting changes go into the Piton source. Generated guidance
1217	is derived from the resolved source and configuration, and implementation is
1218	assessed against the specification. The compiler loads the four constructs and
1219	the three adapters from the spec's own `.pi` files
1220	(`spec/scope/belay/anchors/`, `spec/scope/belay/adapters/`), so the compiler
1221	and the spec can't disagree: changing `Skill.pi` changes the framework.
1222	
1223	### 11.1 Configuration
1224	
1225	A project turns on Belay by listing a `belay-config` anchor under
1226	`frameworks`:
1227	
1228	| Field | Meaning |
1229	| --- | --- |
1230	| `codeRoot` | Required. Where the app's code lives, relative to the project config. |
1231	| `shapeRoot` | Optional. Where the shape instructions live. Without it, `BELAY_SHAPE_ROOT` is the project root and nothing is placed by shape. |
1232	| `adapters` | Required. The adapters to build for: `ClaudeCodeAdapter`, `CodexAdapter`, `OpenCodeAdapter`. |
1233	| `crossDiscovery` | Optional. `separate` when each tool's output is deployed apart (every adapter writes its own complete tree); `allow` to accept that OpenCode offers other tools' command skills as ordinary skills. Without it, the enabled tools share one project (11.5). |
1234	| `instructionByteLimit` | Optional number. The instruction byte limit to check against, for targets that have one. |

1237	`piton.config.pi` lives).

1240	
1241	Every construct extends the abstract `Construct`, whose `description` and
1242	`prompt` are both optional (`:: string:: null: null`). Any other property is
1243	preserved and serialized as Markdown after the prompt.

1246	| --- | --- | --- | --- |

1248	| `skill` | `useWhen:: string` | Instructions the agent loads selectively for one kind of work. | Name from the anchor through the adapter's naming rules. Discovery description is `<description> Use when <useWhen>`. Body is `prompt`, then the extra properties. The platform decides when to load it. |
1249	| `command` | none | An explicit entrypoint that invokes a prompt or directs work through skills. | Name is `x-` plus the normalized name. A native command, or the explicit-invocation equivalent the adapter defines. |
1250	| `agent` | `role:: string` | A role and the instructions for performing it. | Identity is the kebab-case anchor name, unless the target needs another form. The body starts with `You are a <role>`, then the prompt, then the extra properties. |
1251	
1252	- Abstract constructs can supply shared structure. Required fields
1253	  (`useWhen`, `role`) are checked only on concrete constructs, after
1254	  inheritance resolves.
1255	- Description and prompt are left out of the output when missing. **If the
1256	  target needs a description and there isn't one, that is
1257	  `missing-description`**: Claude Code needs one for agents; Codex for skills,
1258	  commands and agents; OpenCode for skills and agents.
1259	- The role introduction is literal: `role: careful reviewer` gives
1260	  `You are a careful reviewer`.
1261	- The skill description is literal too: `description: Reviews code.` with
1262	  `useWhen: asked for a review` gives
1263	  `Reviews code. Use when asked for a review`.

1265	```piton
1266	use @piton/belay
1267	
1268	export skill AnswerSpecQuestions:
1269	    description: Reads the spec and answers questions about it.
1270	    useWhen: asked how part of the specification works
1271	    prompt:
1272	        Read the spec under spec/ and understand the language and features
1273	        before answering.
1274	    reportFormat:
1275	        Save every report as a standalone HTML file.
1276	```

1278	`reportFormat` is an extra property. It renders as a `# Report Format` section
1279	after the prompt.
1280	
1281	**Native options.** Some property names are target metadata rather than prose
1282	and are never serialized into the body: `tools`, `model`, `allowed-tools`,
1283	`mode`, `permission`, `agent`, `model_reasoning_effort` and `sandbox_mode`.
1284	Each adapter supports a subset (11.5). An option the target cannot represent
1285	is `unsupported-option`, and an invalid value is `invalid-option`. How these
1286	are typed is still an open decision (11.7).

1288	### 11.3 Shape mapping (instructions)
1289	
1290	The tree under `shapeRoot` roughly mirrors the tree under `codeRoot`:
1291	
1292	| Source | Existing scope | Generic output |
1293	| --- | --- | --- |
1294	| `spec/shape/components/button/Button.pi` | `src/components/button` | `src/components/button/AGENTS.md` |
1295	| `spec/shape/components/input/Input.pi` and `InputDesign.pi` | `src/components/input` | one combined `src/components/input/AGENTS.md` |
1296	| `spec/shape/components/nonexistent/Component.pi` | `src/components` (walked up) | `src/components/AGENTS.md` |
1297	
1298	- The instruction's directory relative to `shapeRoot` is resolved under
1299	  `codeRoot`. If it is missing, Belay walks upward to the nearest directory
1300	  that exists, **stopping at `codeRoot`**.
1301	- Each adapter uses its own filename: `CLAUDE.md` for Claude Code, `AGENTS.md`
1302	  for Codex and OpenCode. The file holds a heading per instruction
1303	  (`# Button Shape`) and its content.
1304	- Falling back to a parent changes placement only. The shape-reference tree
1305	  (`<referenceRoot>/shape/...`) keeps the original relative location.
1306	- What happens to an instruction outside `shapeRoot` is an open decision, so
1307	  the compiler refuses to guess and reports an error
1308	  (`instruction-placement-unspecified`). Keep instructions under `shapeRoot`.
1309	- Loading differs per tool (11.5), so placement does not guarantee the
1310	  instruction is in the initial context.

1312	### 11.4 References and special imports
1313	
1314	- **Emission.** Belay emits only what the build emits: the entry file's
1315	  exports and anything they reference.
1316	- **Reference tree.** Reached anchors are serialized into the adapter's
1317	  `referenceRoot`, **one Markdown file per source module**, keeping the
1318	  module's path under `root`. Each anchor is a heading in its module's file.
1319	  So `spec/components/Button.pi` becomes
1320	  `.claude/reference/components/Button.md`. The reference tree (and its
1321	  `shape/` subdirectory) is a Belay convention, **not a platform discovery
1322	  directory**: never assume a tool loads it. It is reached only through links.
1323	- `@{X}` in any generated file becomes a relative Markdown link to X's heading
1324	  in that tree, with a `#fragment`:
1325	  `[Button](../../reference/components/Button.md#button)`, or
1326	  `[Button.color](../../reference/components/Button.md#color)`. Links stay lazy
1327	  and are never replaced with Claude's eager `@import` syntax.
1328	- **A reference to a skill, command or agent** links to that construct's own
1329	  output, like its `SKILL.md`, and it isn't copied into the reference tree.
1330	- **Special imports.** Each is imported explicitly from `@piton/belay` and
1331	  resolved **at compile time, separately for each adapter and each output
1332	  file**, as a path relative to the generated file that uses it. Interpolate
1333	  them with `${...}`.
1334	
1335	  | Import | Resolves to |
1336	  | --- | --- |
1337	  | `BELAY_COMPILED_SHAPE` | The compiled copy of the shape for the adapter, under its reference directory (`.claude/reference/shape` for Claude Code). Not the same as `BELAY_SHAPE_ROOT`. |
1338	  | `BELAY_AGENT_ROOT` | The agent's directory: `.claude`, `.codex` or `.opencode`. |
1339	  | `BELAY_PROJECT_ROOT` | The project root, where `piton.config.pi` lives. |
1340	  | `BELAY_SHAPE_ROOT` | The configured `shapeRoot`, or the project root if unset. |
1341	  | `BELAY_CODE_ROOT` | The configured `codeRoot`. |
1342	
1343	  ```piton
1344	  use @piton/belay
1345	
1346	  from @piton/belay import BELAY_COMPILED_SHAPE
1347	
1348	  export skill Designer:
1349	      description: Designs components.
1350	      useWhen: asked to design a component
1351	      prompt: Read the shape documents under ${BELAY_COMPILED_SHAPE} first.
1352	  ```
1353	
1354	  In `.claude/skills/designer/SKILL.md` that becomes
1355	  `../../reference/shape`.
1356	
1357	  Special imports compose like any value:
1358	  `export FLUENCY_PROMPT_FILE: ${BELAY_PROJECT_ROOT}/FLUENCY_PROMPT.md` can
1359	  then be interpolated as `${FLUENCY_PROMPT_FILE}` in a skill prompt. The
1360	  repo's own `spec/agent/` (three skills and `command CheckSpecForProblems`,
1361	  re-exported from `spec/agent/index.pi`) are working examples.

1364	### 11.5 Adapters
1365	
1366	`@piton/belay` exports `ClaudeCodeAdapter`, `CodexAdapter` and
1367	`OpenCodeAdapter`. Each extends the abstract `belay-agent-adapter`
1368	(`description`, `targetId`, `instructionFile`, `referenceRoot`).
1369	
1370	| | Claude Code (`claude-code`) | Codex (`codex`) | OpenCode (`opencode`) |
1371	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
1372	| Instruction file | `CLAUDE.md` | `AGENTS.md` | `AGENTS.md` |
1373	| Reference root | `.claude/reference` | `.codex/reference` | `.opencode/reference` |
1374	| Skill | `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, YAML frontmatter `name`, `description` | `.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, same frontmatter | `.opencode/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`. Name 1–64 lowercase alphanumerics with single hyphens, matching its directory; description 1–1024 characters. |
1375	| Command | Translated: `.claude/skills/x-<name>/SKILL.md` with `disable-model-invocation: true`, invoked as `/x-<name>` | Translated: `.agents/skills/x-<name>/SKILL.md` plus `agents/openai.yaml` with `policy: allow_implicit_invocation: false`, invoked as `$x-<name>` | Native: `.opencode/commands/x-<name>.md`, identity from the filename, invoked as `/x-<name>` |
1376	| Agent | `.claude/agents/<name>.md`, frontmatter `name`, `description`, optional `tools`, `model` | `.codex/agents/<name>.toml` with `name`, `description`, `developer_instructions` (role, prompt, extras), optional `model`, `model_reasoning_effort`, `sandbox_mode` | `.opencode/agents/<name>.md`, frontmatter `description`, `mode` (`primary`, `subagent` or `all`; always explicit, default `subagent`), optional `model`, `permission`; identity from the filename |
1377	| Native options | agent: `tools`, `model`. skill and command: `allowed-tools`, `model`. | agent: `model`, `model_reasoning_effort`, `sandbox_mode`. None for skills or commands. | agent: `mode`, `model`, `permission`. command: `agent`, `model`. None for skills. |
1378	| Loading | Ancestor guidance loads at startup; nested guidance loads when Claude reads in that subtree. | A root-to-working-directory chain is built at run start. A same-directory `AGENTS.override.md` shadows generated guidance (`shadowed-instruction`); an instruction byte limit applies (`instruction-over-budget`). | Searches upward from the working directory and prefers `AGENTS.md` over its `CLAUDE.md` fallback. Nested files are not assumed to load (`unguaranteed-instruction-scope` unless configured). It also discovers Claude and `.agents` skills. |
1379	
1380	Rules for every adapter:
1381	
1382	- **Pipeline:** take the emitted, validated constructs from Piton, build one
1383	  output plan per adapter, resolve instruction placement and reference
1384	  destinations, check shared paths and cross-discovery across the whole plan,
1385	  serialize, validate links, metadata, names and output ownership, then write.
1386	- Every adapter carries `documentationChecked` (currently `2026-09-21`): the
1387	  date its target's documentation was last checked, recorded in the
1388	  manifest's `targets`.
1389	- Constructs are consumed **after** imports and inheritance resolve. Each of
1390	  the four constructs is mapped explicitly for each target.
1391	- An adapter distinguishes native support, translation and unsupported
1392	  behaviour, and fails with an actionable diagnostic when required behaviour
1393	  can't be represented.
1394	- Model and permission settings are applied **only when configured
1395	  explicitly**. Absent settings are omitted so native defaults apply. Native
1396	  options are validated against the target platform version, and role,
1397	  prompt and other prose never get copied into metadata fields.
1398	- **A prompt that requests restraint is not an enforced restriction.** An
1399	  adapter claims enforcement only for controls the platform applies, and never
1400	  translates permissions in a way that silently widens access. Claude's
1401	  `allowed-tools` and subagent `tools` serve different purposes; neither is a
1402	  portable sandbox. Requesting an enforced restriction the adapter can't
1403	  represent is a diagnostic.
1404	- An adapter never silently turns an agent into a skill, or a command into an
1405	  automatically invoked skill, when that changes how it activates.
1406	- Names are normalized before planning, and commands keep the `x-` prefix
1407	  after normalization. Collisions are errors (`name-collision`,
1408	  `output-collision`) unless the artifacts are identical in content,
1409	  reference resolution and activation.
1410	- **Multiple adapters:** the tools read each other's files (Codex and
1411	  OpenCode both read `AGENTS.md`; OpenCode also discovers `.claude/skills` and
1412	  `.agents/skills`), so with several adapters Belay plans one shared project
1413	  and writes each artifact once, where the tools find it:
1414	  - the **first adapter listed owns the one reference tree**, and every
1415	    adapter links into it;
1416	  - an instruction file several adapters place at one path (`AGENTS.md`) is
1417	    **written once**, by the first of them listed;
1418	  - OpenCode **writes no copy of a skill** Claude Code or Codex already
1419	    writes where it discovers it, and links to theirs;
1420	  - a command's `x-` skill that OpenCode would discover is an error
1421	    (`cross-discovery-activation`) unless `opencode.json` hides it with a
1422	    skill permission (`"permission": {"skill": {"x-*": "deny"}}`; the last
1423	    matching pattern decides) or `crossDiscovery` is set;
1424	  - a skill OpenCode finds in two directories (all three adapters enabled)
1425	    is a `cross-target-discovery` warning, since nothing in the project can
1426	    stop it.
1427	
1428	  `crossDiscovery: separate` means each tool's tree is deployed apart: every
1429	  adapter writes its own complete tree, and incompatible writes to one path
1430	  are rejected (`output-collision`). The whole plan is still checked before
1431	  anything is written.
1432	- Generated links (from `@{...}` references) are relative to the file that
1433	  contains them and must point at planned outputs (`broken-reference-link`).
1434	  Markdown links you write in prose are text and are never checked.
1435	- Discovery metadata and body are emitted exactly once. Frontmatter is written
1436	  with a format-aware YAML or TOML encoder. Generated filenames and native
1437	  metadata are checked against the target's schema, and unsupported requested
1438	  capabilities are diagnosed before anything is written.
1439	
1440	Adapter specifics:
1441	
1442	- **Claude Code.** A skill's directory name is its frontmatter `name`. Claude
1443	  Code still reads `.claude/commands/`, but Belay emits commands only as
1444	  skills, never both for one command. Agent identity comes from the
1445	  normalized name, never a rendered heading. `allowed-tools`/`tools` are
1446	  never copied to another platform without a mapping.
1447	- **Codex.** Belay never writes `AGENTS.override.md` to win precedence.
1448	  Guidance below the directory a session starts in is not guaranteed to load.
1449	  The byte limit checked is `instructionByteLimit` (11.1). Commands never use
1450	  deprecated custom prompts or an invented `.codex/commands/`.
1451	  `developer_instructions` is one valid TOML string; a generic `tools` list is
1452	  never mapped to an invented field. Only the standalone custom-agent format is
1453	  targeted. Codex's sandbox and approval settings govern execution and
1454	  guidance can't override them; tool or model settings on a command are
1455	  diagnosed. A command must produce both its files, and an agent's TOML must
1456	  parse with `name`, `description` and `developer_instructions`.
1457	- **OpenCode.** Don't assume Claude's nested loading or Codex's chain. Extra
1458	  guidance files go through its explicit `instructions` configuration when a
1459	  deployment needs them, never by loading every nested instruction globally;
1460	  if shape scoping is required and can't be guaranteed, that is an error.
1461	  Unrecognized frontmatter never enforces policy. `model` values are
1462	  provider-qualified. Argument placeholders written in a command prompt are
1463	  kept. `allowed-tools` is never an enforced command setting. Agents use
1464	  `permission`, not the deprecated `tools`, mapped only when the meaning is
1465	  equivalent: allow/ask/deny is not a tool list, and ambiguous conversions are
1466	  rejected.
1467	
1468	Other Belay diagnostics include `invalid-artifact-name`,
1469	`missing-command-prefix`, `description-too-long`, `output-outside-project`,
1470	`unowned-output`, `duplicated-content` and `unrepresentable-reference`.

1472	### 11.6 Guarantees
1473	
1474	- Identical source, configuration, directory state and toolchain produce
1475	  identical bytes. Instructions combined into one file have a stable order.
1476	- Frontmatter values are quoted and escaped for the target format.
1477	- A missing reference target is reported instead of emitting a broken link.
1478	- Unsupported metadata is reported instead of being claimed as enforced.
1479	- Generated files are tracked in `.piton/manifest.json`, so cleanup never
1480	  deletes files users wrote. Its `targets` records, for each target, the
1481	  documentation date the generated files were validated against.
1482	- Failures name the source anchor and property. Output stays inside its
1483	  configured boundaries.

1486	
1487	`spec/scope/belay/Decisions.pi` lists what is not decided. Tooling should say
1488	it is unspecified rather than guess:
1489	
1490	- Placement of instructions outside `shapeRoot`.
1491	- The types of `tools`, `allowed-tools` and `model`, and their mapping per

1493	- Naming: skill filename normalization, command name normalization before the

1495	- Whether workflows stay compositions of the four constructs. Do not add a
1496	  `workflow` keyword just because examples describe agent processes.
1497	- How platform-specific adapter options are written.

1502	## 12. Package management
1503	
1504	Packages are git repositories, managed as **vendored dependencies**. Installed
1505	packages are stored inside the project and committed to version control, and
1506	the tooling adds, updates, removes and inspects them. Nothing is fetched at
1507	compile time.
1508	
1509	- **Offering packages.** A repository declares packages with `piton-package`
1510	  anchors (`PitonPackage` from `@piton/packaging`: `name`, `root`,
1511	  `dependencies`). A package anchor can live anywhere in the specbase but must
1512	  be listed under `packages:` in `piton.config.pi`. A package's `root` is
1513	  relative to `piton.config.pi`, like the project's own root. **`packages:` is what the
1514	  repository offers to other projects; a project never installs its own
1515	  packages.** One repository can offer several packages, each with its own
1516	  root and dependencies.
1517	- **Names.** `name` is what the package installs under. It exists because it
1518	  can be kebab-case (`my-package`), which an anchor name can't. Left out, the
1519	  anchor's own name is used. **Package names are flat: no `/`.** Names like
1520	  `@piton/belay` are only for the packages bundled with the compiler.
1521	- **Dependencies.** `dependencies:` lists git URLs, each with an optional
1522	  `commit:`, `tag:` or `branch:` on an indented line beneath it (a dictionary
1523	  item right after the URL). **Only one pin per URL**; more is
1524	  `multiple-pins`. Without a pin, the latest commit on the default branch is
1525	  used. **Pins are strings**: `@piton/config` types them as strings, so
1526	  `tag: 1.0` stays `"1.0"`. Other pin diagnostics are `dangling-pin` and
1527	  `unknown-pin`.
1528	- **Picking packages.** A repository can offer several packages. You get all
1529	  of them unless you list the ones you want with `packages:` under the URL:
1530	  `packages: [ui-kit]`.
1531	- **Project and package dependencies are separate.** The project's apply only
1532	  to the project, and each package declares its own.
1533	- **No nested dependencies.** When two packages need the same package at
1534	  different versions, **the one with the newest commit wins** and a warning is
1535	  shown.
1536	- **Installation.** Each package goes into `tethers/<name>`, next to
1537	  `piton.config.pi`, with the files from its `root`. A repository offering
1538	  `ui-kit` and `my-package` gives `tethers/ui-kit` and `tethers/my-package`.
1539	  Tethering removes every trace of git. A repository that offers no packages
1540	  is installed whole, under the name its URL implies.
1541	- **Importing.** An installed package is a location placeholder:
1542	  `from my-package import X`, `use my-package`, `use my-package/MyAnchor`.
1543	  Normal path resolution applies below it. A missing package is a compiler
1544	  error.
1545	- **Lock file.** `.piton/tether.lock`, next to `piton.config.pi`, keeps each
1546	  tethered package's URL, commit and a hash of its files. `tether` and
1547	  `update` write it, and it is committed with the project.
1548	- **Conflicts.** Before tether, update or any other operation on an installed
1549	  package, the tooling compares its files with the lock file and goes ahead
1550	  only if nothing changed. If the files were edited, it says so and asks the
1551	  user to untether (or `piton update --force` to discard the edits).
1552	
1553	The commands:
1554	
1555	- `piton tether` on its own installs everything in `dependencies`. Given a
1556	  source URL, it adds it to `dependencies` in `piton.config.pi` and installs
1557	  it. `--as <name>` installs under another name.
1558	- `piton update [packages...] [--force] [--diff]` reinstalls from
1559	  `dependencies`, all packages when none are named. `--force` replaces a
1560	  package even if it was edited, discarding the edits with a warning;
1561	  `--diff` prints a coloured unified diff of every file each update changed.
1562	- `piton untether <package>` moves the package from `tethers/` to
1563	  `<root>/untethered/` and rewrites the imports that named it, making it the
1564	  project's own source. `--as <name>` renames it; `--no-rewrite` only moves
1565	  it.
1566	- `piton remove <package>` deletes an installed package and removes it from
1567	  `dependencies`. It refuses if the files were edited or if anything still
1568	  imports the package.

1570	## 13. CLI reference
1571	
1572	Every command prints what it produced first, then a one-line outcome (✓ or
1573	✗), and its problems last: diagnostics, errors and warnings with their help
1574	and notes, then the error and warning count. On a terminal the output is
1575	coloured and paths are marked `+`/`-`; piped or with `NO_COLOR`, it is plain
1576	text and stdout carries the bare results.
1577	
1578	| Command | Behaviour |
1579	| --- | --- |
1580	| `piton check [paths...]` | Validates syntax, imports, references, types, inheritance, composition, exports and circular dependencies, reporting errors and warnings. Writes nothing. Exits 0 when there are no errors and 1 otherwise. Paths are optional files, directories or globs; the default is the project (or every `.pi` file under the working directory when there's no `piton.config.pi`). |
1581	| `piton build [config] [--dry-run]` | Builds the project configured by `piton.config.pi` (or the given config). Writes renderer output to `<output>/<path under root>.<ext>` (defaults: `./dist`, JSON), so `spec/components/Button.pi` becomes `dist/components/Button.json`: the entry file plus every file holding something the entry's exports reference. A registered framework's output replaces it unless the config sets `output` or `renderer`, which asks for both. Records every file in `.piton/manifest.json`. The whole plan is validated before anything is written. `--dry-run` reports without writing. |
1582	| `piton compile <path> [--renderer json\|yaml\|markdown] [--write] [--dependencies]` | Compiles one file to stdout (JSON by default): one key per export. `--write` writes `<file>.<ext>` next to each input and is required for globs. `--dependencies` wraps the result as `{"value": "<compiled output as a string>", "dependencies": [absolute source paths]}` so build tools know what to watch; bundled package files are left out. |
1583	| `piton format [path] [--check]` | Applies canonical formatting (4-space indents, constraint spacing, sorted and wrapped imports, no `.pi` in import paths, a space after `//`). `--check` reports without writing. `piton format -` reads source from stdin and writes the formatted text to stdout. It **only splits overflowing lines and never rejoins a paragraph**, so rewrap edited prose by hand, and don't reflow `key: value` blocks as prose. |
1584	| `piton reach [targets...] [--no-unreachable] [--no-paths]` | Starting from files, globs or anchor names (the entry by default), follows outgoing imports, references, inheritance and composition, direct and transitive. Reports what is reachable with its depth and the path taken, and what is unreachable. The flags hide the last two. Use it to find dead spec. Grouped by source, with a summary. No diagnostics; always exits 0. |
1585	| `piton slice <target> [--adapter <target>]` | Prints the part of the spec one thing depends on, as one Markdown document for an agent's prompt. The target is `file.pi#Anchor`, `file.pi#Anchor.property`, `file.pi#variable`, or a bare name looked up across the project (an error when more than one file declares it). Follows, transitively: what an anchor extends, every base that also declares a property, anchors named by type constraints, what a value read (`${Other.x}`, variables), and what it references or embeds. Imports alone bring nothing in. A whole anchor needs all its properties and bases; slicing a property leaves out the anchor's other properties; a reference to a property needs only that property. It also includes the **chain** from the project's entry down to the target (`Specification.Tooling`, `Tooling.cli`, `Cli.commands`): the shortest path the build takes, each link only that one property and not followed further. An export of the entry, a variable, and a file the build doesn't reach have no chain. Order: the target, then its dependencies nearest first (source order breaks ties), then the chain outermost first, so the same source prints the same bytes. Each declaration appears once, headed by its name as written (`SaveButton.color`), with its file, what it extends, its type and what it reads. References and embeds are written as names; cycles are followed until they come back around. Every path it prints is relative to the directory it runs in, and it finds the project by looking upward for `piton.config.pi`. `--adapter claude-code` (any Belay target the project builds) cites the compiled output instead: each location and every reference links to where `piton build` writes it (an embedded anchor to the section that embeds it), and no `.pi` file is ever cited; an abstract base or an anchor that is only read has no document of its own and is described without one. With `--adapter` the target itself must be something the build writes out. Markdown links the author wrote pass through unchanged. Exits 1 on errors. |
1586	| `piton init [directory] [--template <group/name>] [--adapter <id>...] [--list]` | Starts a new project from a template compiled into the compiler (no network needed). Templates come in groups: `piton/minimal` (plain Piton to JSON), `piton/library` (a package others can tether), `belay/application` (a shape instruction placed in `src/`, a skill, an agent and a command) and `belay/minimal` (the Belay config and one skill). Without a directory it first asks for the project's name and creates that directory (an empty answer, or no terminal, uses the working one). Then it asks for a group and a template (`--template belay` asks only for the template), and for a Belay template, which adapters to build for: a checklist of Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode with the template's default (Claude Code) checked, or `--adapter`, repeated or comma-separated. The chosen adapters replace the config's import and `adapters` list, and a template's `.adapters/<id>/` files (like OpenCode's `opencode.json`) are written only for the adapters chosen. Templates are the `group/name` directories in the compiler repo's `create-templates/`, each with a one-line `.template` description that is not written out; adding one is adding a directory, and every template must check cleanly, be formatted, and build. `--list` describes the groups and templates and does nothing else. With no terminal, a full template name is required. It never overwrites a file: if any it would write exists, it names each and writes none, and cancelling a question writes nothing. Prints each written path on stdout, then a summary and the next commands on stderr. Exits 1 on errors. |
1587	| `piton loc [paths...]` | Counts total, code, comment and blank lines per file, with a summary. Defaults to the project. No diagnostics; always exits 0. |
1588	| `piton lsp` | Runs the language server over stdio (section 14). |
1589	| `piton agent [claude] [--print-fluency] [args...]` | Launches the agent with a short project primer plus this fluency prompt (the project's `FLUENCY_PROMPT.md`, or the copy built into the compiler), passed to `claude` as `--append-system-prompt`. Extra arguments go to the agent. `--print-fluency` prints the prompt and does nothing else. |
1590	| `piton tether [source] [--as name]` | See section 12. |
1591	| `piton update [packages...] [--force] [--diff]` | See section 12. |
1592	| `piton untether <package> [--as name] [--no-rewrite]` | See section 12. |
1593	| `piton remove <package>` | See section 12. |
1594	
1595	Each CLI command in the spec is a `cli-command` anchor
1596	(`spec/scope/tooling/cli/index.pi`) with `commandName`, `positionalArguments`
1597	and `namedArguments`.
1598	
1599	## 14. Language server, editors, and JavaScript
1600	
1601	`piton lsp` provides, from the spec's feature list:
1602	
1603	- Diagnostics (not for missing optional properties), completion, hover (type,
1604	  source, documentation, inheritance chain, export status and compiled
1605	  interpretation), go-to-definition, find-references, and rename across the
1606	  whole specbase.
1607	- Auto-import, import organization, and code actions: import a missing
1608	  symbol, create an unresolved anchor, add an export, qualify an ambiguous
1609	  reference, resolve a simple inheritance conflict.
1610	- Document and workspace symbols, semantic highlighting, inlay hints
1611	  (resolved types, inherited origins, composition sources), formatting,
1612	  folding and selection ranges.
1613	- Inheritance, composition (`+`, `++`), override and conflict resolution;
1614	  reference resolution; validation and type information for expressions in
1615	  `{}`, `${}`, `#{}` and `@{}`; export validation; module resolution; cycle
1616	  detection (circular imports are fine and not reported).
1617	- Related-symbol navigation, a hierarchy view, resolved-value and provenance
1618	  inspection, compiled-output preview, source-to-output mapping, unused and
1619	  redundant definition detection, and documentation integration.
1620	- Incremental analysis and workspace indexing.
1621	- Diagnostics cover Belay semantics as well as Piton. Import organization
1622	  flags unused, duplicate, invalid and overly broad imports. Cycle detection
1623	  also catches an anchor that ends up extending itself, and shows the cycle.
1624	
1625	There is no signature help.
1626	
1627	Completion rules: never suggest things that don't exist; offer nothing on an
1628	empty value (`property: `), because prose probably follows; offer nothing
1629	after a `.` inside a string.
1630	
1631	Editing rules every editor must follow, through the LSP or the editor
1632	extension:
1633	
1634	- Enter after a colon that opens a dictionary or anchor property starts a new
1635	  line indented one level deeper.
1636	- Enter on a blank line inside a dictionary or anchor starts a new line one
1637	  level shallower.
1638	- Format-on-save is optional. It adds the space after `//` and touches nothing
1639	  else that is commented.
1640	
1641	Supported editors and their highlighters (spec): VS Code (TextMate plus LSP);
1642	Emacs, Helix and Zed (tree-sitter plus LSP); Neovim and Vim (vim syntax);
1643	JetBrains (`jetbrains`); Sublime (sublime-syntax); Kate (KSyntaxHighlighting).
1644	Every editor gets full LSP support. The integrations live under `editors/`.
1645	
1646	**Consuming Piton from JavaScript.** `packages/vite-plugin-piton` imports
1647	`.pi` files as modules, with HMR, dependency tracking (through
1648	`piton compile --dependencies`) and virtual modules. Each export in the Piton
1649	file is a named export, and the default export is the whole file, the same as
1650	`piton compile` gives:
1651	
1652	```ts
1653	import { SaveButton } from '../spec/app.pi';
1654	import spec from '../spec/app.pi';
1655	
1656	const button = SaveButton;
1657	const cancel = spec.CancelButton;
1658	```
1659	
1660	It has a configurable default renderer (`renderer: 'json' | 'yaml' |
1661	'markdown'`), and the renderers can also be imported as functions
1662	(`vite-plugin-piton/renderers`) and used inline. `packages/astro-piton` is an
1663	Astro integration that wraps the Vite plugin.
1664	
1665	## 15. Working on a specbase
1666	
1667	1. **Orient.** Open `piton.config.pi` to find `root`, `entry`, `output`, the
1668	   frameworks, the adapters, `codeRoot` and `shapeRoot`. Read the entry file,
1669	   usually `spec/index.pi`, because its exports are the compilation roots.
1670	   Follow the `index.pi` files down through the modules. In this repository,
1671	   `spec/index.pi` exports `Specification` (FoundingThesis, Language, Tooling,
1672	   Belay, PackageManagement) plus the skills and command in `spec/agent/`.
1673	2. **Read compiled reference for overview, and source for truth.**
1674	   `<referenceRoot>/**/*.md` is easy to browse, and its links are lazy, so
1675	   follow them only when relevant.
1676	3. **Edit the `.pi` source**, following the conventions around it:
1677	   - one exported anchor per file, named after the file;
1678	   - `index.pi` files that re-export with `from ./X export *`;
1679	   - abstract anchors exported with a keyword, and shared abstracts in a
1680	     `lib/` folder;
1681	   - lowerCamelCase property names;
1682	   - SCREAMING_CASE for exported constant lists;
1683	   - prose in string blocks, and structure in keys and lists;
1684	   - `@{X}` to link related documents;
1685	   - examples inside fences wrapped in a `\\\` escape block.
1686	4. **Keep imports honest.** Use `use` for keywords and `from ... import` for
1687	   names; a file often needs both. A new file only compiles if the entry
1688	   reaches it, so export it through an index or reference it.
1689	5. **Validate.**
1690	   - Run `piton check`.
1691	   - `piton check` does **not** compile the examples inside escape blocks
1692	     (they are literal text). When you edit spec examples, extract each ` ```piton ` block,
1693	     run `piton compile` on it, and compare with any ` ```json ` block that
1694	     follows. Remember that compile output has only exported names.
1695	   - Run `piton build`, then look at the diff of the generated files.
1696	   - Run `piton reach` to confirm new anchors are reached.
1697	   - Run `piton format --check`.
1698	6. **Never hand-edit generated files.** That includes `CLAUDE.md` and
1699	   `AGENTS.md` under `codeRoot`, everything under `.claude/`, `.codex/`,
1700	   `.agents/`, `.opencode/` and the build output directory that is listed in
1701	   `.piton/manifest.json`, and the files in `.piton/` themselves.
1702	7. **Keep implementation and spec in agreement.** The implementation is judged
1703	   against the spec. When they disagree, report it instead of quietly bending
1704	   the spec to fit. Trust `piton compile` for how things behave today, and
1705	   flag the gap.
1706	
1707	## 16. Where the compiler differs from the spec
1708	
1709	Checked with `piton compile` and `piton build`:
1710	
1711	- The CLI has a few things the spec doesn't name: `build --dry-run`,
1712	  `tether --as`, agent argument passthrough, the `reach` flags, and
1713	  `format` with no path or `-`.
1714	
1715	- **Paragraph breaks.** The spec says a blank line in a string block starts a
1716	  new paragraph. The compiler joins the paragraphs with a single `\n`, which
1717	  Markdown output renders as one paragraph with a soft line break.
1718	
1719	Known limitations, where the spec is silent and the compiler's choice may
1720	surprise you:
1721	
1722	- A `/`-rooted import inside an installed package resolves against the
1723	  consuming project's root, not the package's. Use relative imports inside a
1724	  package.
1725	- A required property from an abstract is not satisfied by a value inherited
1726	  from a concrete base (`needs Thing extends Base`, where `Base` supplies it):
1727	  the keyword's anchor comes last, and its value-less declaration wins. Give
1728	  the value on the anchor itself.
1729	- `piton check` with no paths checks what the entry reaches, so a file that
1730	  nothing imports is not checked. Name it: `piton check path/to/file.pi`.
1731	- **Prose directly in an anchor body is silently dropped.** `anchor A:` with
1732	  only a line of text under it (no key) compiles to an empty anchor, with no
1733	  diagnostic. Always put prose under a key, such as `description:`.
1734	- Mixed-type equality is simply unequal: `{1 == "1"}` is `false`, not an
1735	  error. The spec says `==` works on every type but doesn't spell this out.
1736	- Which constructs each adapter requires a `description` for (section 11.2)
1737	  is hardcoded in `crates/piton-belay/src/adapter.rs`, not declared in the
1738	  adapter `.pi` files.

# Theme Scope

## Concept

### Pitch

The look every part of the application shares: a gentle, neutral grey interface in the manner of Photoshop, Maya, or Houdini, where contrast alone says what matters, and colour is kept for meaning.

### Shape

#### Description

The theme is defined by its dark mode, built around a base grey of #444444. Dark mode is the reference: every colour below is chosen for it first, and light mode is its reasonable interpretation on a light base, keeping the same roles, the same order, and steps of about the same size. The greys are true neutrals, with no hint of blue or warmth. There are no gradients, and no texture. Everything that uses a colour names its role here rather than a value of its own, so the two modes stay coherent.

#### Hierarchy

How far a colour is from the base, in contrast, says how much it stands out, and that holds everywhere. The base is the quiet ground of the window. A step away is structure: panels, controls, and the lines between them. Further away is what is worked on: text, content, and the wells that hold it. Furthest away is state and meaning: what is selected, focused, or needs attention. Nothing structural is ever further from the base than the content it frames, and nothing decorative is ever as far as state. A hover is always a smaller step than a selection, and a selection a smaller step than focus.

#### Surfaces

Each surface in dark mode, then light mode:

- well, #2e2e2e, then #f5f5f5: where content is read or written, such as the editor, code blocks, answers, and task tables' bodies; the most contrast with the text it holds
- recessed, #383838, then #e8e8e8: text inputs, lists, and trees, a step toward the well
- base, #444444, then #d0d0d0: the window, its panels, the sidebar, and the ribbon's command area
- raised, #4e4e4e, then #dadada: buttons, tab bars, headers, and cards, a small step toward the viewer
- hover, #585858, then #e2e2e2: a raised or listed thing under the pointer, one step further along the way it is already raised
- pressed, #3c3c3c, then #c6c6c6: a control held down, a step back past the base
- selected, #5e5e5e, then #bcbcbc: a selected row or tab without focus, the neutral state furthest from its surface short of the accent
- overlay, #4a4a4a, then #dcdcdc: floating surfaces, such as menus, popovers, tooltips, the completion menu, and inset panels

#### Light Mode

Light mode reads the dark ladder on a light base of #d0d0d0. Wells and inputs go lighter, toward white, so they keep the most contrast with the dark text they hold, just as they are darker in dark mode for the same reason. Raised controls and floating surfaces go a smaller step lighter too, so they still come forward, and hover goes further the same way. Pressed and selected go darker, and so do lines. Text is dark on light.

#### Text

Text in dark mode, then light mode:

- primary, #ebebeb, then #1e1e1e: the foreground, for anything read
- secondary, #c4c4c4, then #454545: what the spec calls muted, such as paths, counts, and descriptions
- tertiary, #9c9c9c, then #636363: dimmer than muted, such as help text and placeholders
- disabled, #7a7a7a, then #8c8c8c: what can't be used now

#### Lines

Lines are one pixel, and quieter than anything they separate:

- line, #3a3a3a, then #bdbdbd: dividers between areas, table rows, and list rows
- edge, #2a2a2a, then #a6a6a6: the border of controls, inputs, and floating surfaces, darker than the base in both modes, what the spec calls the border colour

A line is never doubled. Wherever two things that each have a border meet, a single line is drawn between them, never two side by side: one of them leaves that side out, or the two overlap so their lines lie on the same pixels. A thing that fills what holds it leaves out the sides the holder already draws, and a row in a stack draws only the line between it and the row before. This holds while things move too, such as a row sliding into a stack, apart from a frame or two. A focus ring, or an accent bar marking what is current, isn't a border in this sense, and may sit against one. A gpui-kit component used with its default styling, such as tabs in a tab bar, keeps its own borders as gpui-kit draws them; only its colours are the theme's.

#### Accent

One accent, a calm blue, is the only colour that means selection, focus, or the primary action:

- accent, #7fb4ea, then #1f5fa6: focus rings, the underline of a selected tab, links, a selection's edge, and accent text
- accent fill, #3d6a98, then #2b68ad: primary buttons, with primary text in white in both modes, and a selected item in a focused list
- selection, the accent fill at 35% over its surface: selected text

What the spec calls the theme's primary colour, or its focus ring colour, is the accent.

#### Status

Status colours are kept for what they mean, readable as text on the base and every surface darker than it in dark mode, and on the base and every surface lighter than it in light mode:

- success, #8fd095, then #2c6e31: done, added, aligned
- warning, #e6bb68, then #8a5a00: running out, modified, drifting
- error, #f0928a, then #b3261e: failed, removed, diverged
- information, the accent: running, informational notes

Two more hues, for telling kinds of things apart rather than for status:

- purple, #bba0e6, then #6b4aa6
- cyan, #78c8ce, then #1f6f78

Wherever the spec names a hue for what is shown, it means the theme's: blue is the accent, green success, amber or yellow warning, red error, purple and cyan the hues above, and grey tertiary text.
A tint of a colour, such as a prompt mode's or a changed line's, is that colour laid over its surface at low strength, never enough to take the text on it below its contrast.

#### Bevel

A surface that should lift slightly off what it sits on, such as a scrollbar's thumb or a table's header, can have the theme's bevel: a very slight 1 pixel edge around it, just enough to lift it. Its top and left edges are a touch lighter, as white laid faintly over the surface, 8% in dark mode and 55% in light mode; its bottom and right edges only barely darker, as black laid very faintly over it, 6% in dark mode and 3% in light mode, far subtler than the light and never reading as a line. Laid over rather than a colour of its own, it looks the same on any surface, hovered, pressed, or tinted. The lit top runs the full width, and the lit left side runs beneath it; the shaded bottom runs the full width, and the shaded right side runs above it, so no two edges overlap. It sits inside the surface, taking no room, and isn't a border in the sense of lines never being doubled.
A surface being pressed in can have the bevel pressed instead: the same edges, with the light and shade swapped, so its top and left edges are barely darker and its bottom and right edges a touch lighter.

#### Elevation

Floating surfaces sit on the overlay surface with an edge border, and are the only things with a shadow: soft, short, and black, stronger in dark mode than in light. Behind a modal surface, such as an inset panel, the window is dimmed with black, 40% in dark mode and 25% in light mode.

#### Contrast

However the colours are used, primary and secondary text keep at least 4.5 to 1 against the base, recessed, well, and overlay surfaces, and primary text at least 4 to 1 on controls in any state. Tertiary text, status colours, and the accent keep at least 3 to 1 on the base. Edges keep about 1.5 to 1 against the base, and lines less.

#### Gpui Kit

The application's gpui-kit theme is set from these roles in both modes, so a component with gpui-kit's default styling follows the theme with nothing of its own: its background is the base, its foreground primary text, its muted foreground secondary text, its border the edge, its input and list backgrounds recessed, its popover the overlay, its primary and ring the accent, and its success, warning, and danger the status colours.

#### Modes

Which mode shows is up to the application: see the [MainWindowScope](../../scope/application/MainWindow.md#main-window-scope).

# Project Indicator

## How To Build

A ProjectIndicator should be built as a reusable component that will be reused throughout the rest of the codebase.  A component is configurable through arguments or properties that alter its behaviour, appearance, and details.  A ProjectIndicator should encapsulate all of its own reusable behaviour, while leaving the wiring, intergration, and integration to the domain of the application.

## Theme

Drawn in the [ThemeScope](../../theme/index.md#theme-scope): its surfaces, text, lines, accent, and status colours are the theme's roles, named as the theme names them, in both dark and light mode, never colours of its own.

## Concept

### Pitch

Shows which project is loaded, at a glance, wherever it sits.

### Shape

#### Description

A solid block, the full height of wherever it sits, in its own colour: pure black in dark mode, darker than every surface around it, and a text input's background, the theme's well surface, in light mode. It has no border and no rounded corners. In it, a small folder icon, then the name of the project open through the [ProjectDirectoryScope](../../../scope/project-directory/index.md#project-directory-scope), which is its folder's name, in medium weight, vertically centred. The whole block is what is clicked, filling it edge to edge, square, and it highlights on hover.

#### No Project

While no project is open, as the [NoProjectStateScope](../../../scope/no-project/index.md#no-project-state-scope) says, it reads "No project", muted, after the same icon, and has no tooltip.

#### Tooltip

While a project is open, its tooltip gives the project's full path.

#### Recent Projects

Clicking it, or pressing <Ctrl+R> (<Cmd+R> on macOS) anywhere in the window, opens a list of the recent projects of the [ProjectDirectoryScope](../../../scope/project-directory/index.md#project-directory-scope), up to five, newest first; doing so again closes it. Like the palette, the shortcut does nothing while an inset panel is open.
The list hangs flush from the indicator: its top edge is the indicator's bottom edge and its left edge the indicator's, at least 360 pixels wide. It is a solid block in the indicator's own colour, with no rounded corners, and a thin edge along its sides and bottom but none along its top, where it meets the indicator. While it is open, the rest of the window is dimmed as behind an inset panel, and the indicator stays undimmed above the dimming, so the two read as one.
At the top of the list, a filter field with a search icon takes the keyboard as the list opens. Typing filters the projects fuzzily, as the palette matches, by folder name or full path, the best matches first; with nothing typed, all of them show, newest first. <Up> and <Down> move a highlight through the rows, wrapping around, starting on the first row whenever the filter changes, and <Enter> picks the highlighted row.
Each project is a row with its folder name in medium weight above its full path, muted, after a folder icon, or a tick for the project open now. A busy project, of the [OpenProjectsScope](../../../scope/open-projects/index.md#open-projects-scope), shows a small spinner at the right end of its row, and beneath its path, muted, what is running in it, such as "Task running", "2 questions running", or "Building the spec", joined with a middle dot. A busy project is listed even when it is no longer among the five most recent, after them. Rows reach the list's edges, with no rounded corners, and highlight on hover. Picking a row, by clicking or <Enter>, closes the list and switches to that project, or just closes it for the one already open. Switching never stops what is running in the project switched from. Once switched, the chat input takes the keyboard, ready to write to the project switched to. Clicking the indicator, clicking the dimmed window, or <Escape> closes it.
The last row, beneath a thin divider, whatever the filter leaves, reads "Open Project…" after a folder icon, and closes the list and opens the [OpenProjectScope](../../../scope/project/open-project/index.md#open-project-scope).

#### Width

A name wider than 320 pixels is cut off with an ellipsis.

#### Following

It always shows the project open now: opening, creating, or switching to another project changes it straight away.

#### Busy Elsewhere

While another open project is busy, a small dot in the accent colour sits after the name, and the tooltip adds how many other projects are busy.

input.message:
The ribbon is restyled to match the mockup in dark mode: sizes, gaps and colours come out pixel-exact in a captured frame. `cargo build` is clean and all 11 ribbon tests pass. Nothing was committed, and nothing in spec/, .claude/ or CLAUDE.md was touched.

## What changed

**src/theme.rs:31-36, 73-76, 105-108**
- Two new theme colours: `ribbon` for the command area and open tab, and `ribbon_tabs` for the tab row and group dividers.
- Dark: #222222 and #333333.
- Light: #d0d0d0 and #bfbfbf. The tab row is a step darker than the command area there, so the buttons (white laid 45% over) stay clearly apart. The spec doesn't give light values, so this is my reading of "the same steps reversed".

**src/ribbon/mod.rs**
- **Sizes (:49-68):** tab row 32px, tab padding 8px, body padding 8px, gap 4px, divider 4px wide, slim buttons 27px, collapsed small buttons 22px. The title-strip constants and the rotated-title code are gone, and so is the line along the bottom of the tab row.
- **Buttons (`render_command`):**
  - Slim buttons are 27px and small ones 22px.
  - A full button has its small icon centred above a normal-size label, with 8px either side.
  - Custom-variant buttons draw no border.
- **Tabs (:666-716):** gpui-kit's tabs are replaced with flat ones. Each is just its label with 8px either side, and has an accessibility role, label and selected state.
  - A closed tab has no background, only a faint hover overlay.
  - The open tab takes the command area's colour.
  - Code and Spec keep their label colours and their tint over the open tab.
- **Tab row:** a plain row in the tab-row colour.
- **Command area (:781):** 8px padding on all sides, 4px gaps, background #222222, or that colour with the mode tint when Code or Spec is open alone.
- **`group` (:823):** no title strip; the group name is kept as an accessibility label.
- **`divider` (:880):** a 4px bar with rounded ends in the tab-row colour, as tall as the buttons, with the group name as its tooltip.
- **Colour helpers:**
  - `ribbon_colors` (:895) and `tab_hover` (:905).
  - `command_shades` (:917): in dark mode, white is laid over the area just enough to reach #444444. Hover still lightens and pressed still darkens.
- **Collapsed row:** 32px, the same height as the tab row, with the command-area background. The left and right containers are also 32px.

**src/ribbon/application_tab.rs:41:** the collapsed dark-mode switch uses the 22px small height.

## Where it differs from the mockup, or needed a judgement call
- **Project indicator:** it stays pure black, not the mockup's #111111, because the project-indicator spec says pure black in dark mode.
- **Collapse chevron:** kept after the indicator, as you said, so the tabs start 22px further right than in the mockup.
- **Tab and label widths:** tests use a stand-in text system, so the frame gives the Project tab as 75px against the mockup's 61px. I can't confirm real text widths without running the app.
- **Text colour:** labels use the theme's text colour, #ebebeb, where the mockup shows #dddddd.
- **Dividers between tabs' groups:** the spec's "Opening Several Tabs" paragraph still says "no divider between one tab's groups and the next, as between any groups", which conflicts with the rewritten Groups section. I put a divider between every pair of adjacent groups, including across tabs. That spec sentence needs a fix.
- **Which group a tooltip names:** each divider's tooltip names the group after it, so the first group has no tooltip. Every group still carries its name as an accessibility label.
- **Bottom border and theme text:** I kept the ribbon's own 1px line along its bottom, which the mockup crop doesn't show. The theme spec still says the base (#444444) is "the ribbon's command area", which is now stale.

## Tests
Updated in src/main_window.rs:
- `the_ribbon_body_fits_its_commands`: 74px maximum body, 58px full button.
- `ribbon_tabs_are_drawn_beside_the_project_indicator`: flat tabs with no border anywhere in the tab row.
- `ribbon_mode_tabs_are_tinted_like_the_chat_inputs`: finds tabs by id, and the tinted body is the command area plus the tint.
- `ribbon_buttons_are_full_or_slim_and_square`: 27px slims 4px apart, no title strip, borderless, and #444444 on #222222.
- `ribbon_tabs_hold_their_controls`: dividers 4px from the groups on each side, a 32px collapsed row, and 22px small buttons.
- The `layout_tests` unit tests in src/ribbon/mod.rs, for 27, 4 and 58px.

New:
- `ribbon_groups_are_parted_by_dividers`: on the Spec tab in dark and light, no divider before the first group, each divider 4px wide, 4px from the buttons, 58px tall, rounded, and in the tab-row colour on the tinted body. The tooltip text itself isn't tested.
- `ribbon_tab_row_and_open_tab_take_their_own_colours`: exact #333333 and #222222 in dark, the tab row darker than the command area in light, and a closed tab showing the row colour. A pixel walk down the open tab into the commands finds no line.

**Results:**
- Ribbon tests: 11 passed.
- Theme tests: 4 passed.
- Full suite: 347 passed, 4 failed, 1 ignored.
  - Known unrelated failures: `defaults_are_this_repositorys_templates` and `selected_answer_text_can_be_copied_or_attached`.
  - Also failed under full-suite load, but both pass when run alone: `prompt_mode::tests::long_output_is_measured_a_few_rows_a_frame` ("4143 of 1500 rows were drawn in the first frame") and `prompt_mode::tests::previous_tasks_can_be_selected_and_sent_to_the_other_mode`. They look like timing flakes in the uncommitted prompt_mode work.

## Comparison with the mockup
I captured frames with `src/frame_image.rs` through a temporary test, since removed, at 1920px wide and scale 1. The helper draws only boxes and colours, not text or icons.
- **Geometry matches exactly:** tab row 0-32, command area 32-106 (74px), slims at y=40 and 71 (27px each, 4px apart), full buttons 40-98 (58px), buttons starting at x=8, and dividers 4×58 at y=40 with 4px either side.
- **Colours match exactly:** tab row #333333, open tab and command area #222222 with nothing between them, buttons #444444, dividers #333333.
- 89% of pixels are identical to the mockup overall. The rest are text, the chevron offset and the different buttons on each tab.

Images are in /tmp: ribbon-dark-project.png, ribbon-dark-multi.png, ribbon-dark-spec.png and ribbon-light-project.png. In these the indicator shows its hover colour because the test pointer sits at (0,0).

The ribbon now matches your mockup in dark mode: sizes, gaps and colours come out pixel-for-pixel the same in a captured frame. The 11 ribbon tests pass when I run them. Nothing is committed.

**What changed:**
- **Tab row:** 32px tall on #333333, with flat tabs that are just their labels, with no borders or lines. The open tab uses the command area's #222222, so the two read as one piece. Code and Spec keep their coloured labels and tints.
- **Buttons:** #444444, square and borderless.
  - Stacked buttons are 27px tall with 4px between them.
  - Full buttons are 58px tall, with a small icon above the label.
  - Buttons sit 4px apart, and the command area is 74px tall with 8px padding.
- **Groups:** the rotated title strips are gone. Groups are now separated by a 4px rounded bar in the tab-row colour, and hovering a bar shows the next group's name.

The spec is updated in `spec/ui/components/ribbon/index.pi`, the Code and Spec tab colour sections, and the theme; check, format check and build all pass.

**Where it still differs from the mockup:**
- **Collapse chevron:** it still sits after "suspense", as the spec requires, so the tabs start 22px further right. If you want it gone, say so and I'll change the spec.
- **"suspense" background:** it stays pure black rather than #111111, because the project indicator's spec says black.
- **Bottom line:** a 1px line still runs along the bottom of the ribbon; the mockup is cropped too tight to show whether it should be there.
- **Label text:** labels use the theme's text colour (#ebebeb, the mockup has #dddddd). Label widths aren't confirmed, because the tests don't render real text; worth a look in the running app.
- **Light mode:** the light colours were chosen by the coding agent, since the mockup only shows dark: tab row #bfbfbf, command area #d0d0d0.

**Tests:** the full suite has four failures, none from this change. Two are known: `defaults_are_this_repositorys_templates` and `selected_answer_text_can_be_copied_or_attached`. The other two only fail when the whole suite runs at once: `long_output_is_measured_a_few_rows_a_frame` and `previous_tasks_can_be_selected_and_sent_to_the_other_mode`.

There's a large amount of uncommitted work now, everything since the usage popover, so it would be worth committing soon.

The Gmail, Google Calendar and Google Drive connectors still need authorizing in your claude.ai connector settings. The `backlog` MCP server still can't connect because its executable isn't on your PATH.
